title: Surgery without pain

confidence.note: The Boston operation is documented in hospital records and in Henry Bigelow's report of November 1846, and ether's rapid spread is well recorded. Who deserves credit was bitterly contested at the time and still is, and some of the most famous details, such as Warren's 'no humbug' remark, appear only in later, self-serving accounts.

people: William T. G. Morton, Boston dentist who gave the ether
John Collins Warren, surgeon who operated
Edward Gilbert Abbott (b. 1825), the patient
Crawford Williamson Long, Georgia physician who used ether from 1842
Horace Wells (1815–1848), dentist who tried nitrous oxide
James Young Simpson (1811–1870), Edinburgh obstetrician who introduced chloroform
summary: A Boston dentist held a globe of ether vapor to a young man's face while a surgeon cut into his neck, and within months operating rooms around the world fell quiet.
body: On 16 October 1846, in the operating theater of Massachusetts General Hospital, a Boston dentist named William T. G. Morton held a glass globe of sulfuric ether vapor to the face of Edward Gilbert Abbott, a 21-year-old with a congenital mass under his jaw. The surgeon John Collins Warren then cut into his neck. Abbott did not cry out, though he moved and muttered, and afterwards said the pain had been "considerable, though mitigated," as if his skin had been scratched with a hoe. Until then, operations had been done with little or no effective pain relief.

What made the day matter was publicity. Henry Bigelow reported four operations under ether on 18 November; on 3 December a steamer carried the news to Britain, and by the end of the month ether was being used there and in France. Within a year it had reached many countries, though it was not adopted everywhere at once, even in Boston, because early doctors also saw how dangerous it could be.

Morton was not the first. Crawford Long, a Georgia physician, had used ether in operations from 1842 but did not publish. Horace Wells, Morton's former partner, had a tooth pulled under nitrous oxide in December 1844, but his demonstration in Boston was jeered as a "humbug affair" when the patient cried out. The Harvard chemist Charles Jackson had advised Morton on ether. Morton patented the method in November 1846 and campaigned for decades to be named sole discoverer; in 1870 the American Medical Association gave the honor to Wells instead.

A rival agent came quickly. In Edinburgh on 4 November 1847, James Young Simpson and two assistants tried chloroform on themselves, and within 11 days he had published about 50 cases. It was easier to give than ether but could kill without warning: a 15-year-old, Hannah Greener, died under it in January 1848 during removal of a toenail. When John Snow gave chloroform to Queen Victoria at the births of Prince Leopold in 1853 and Princess Beatrice in 1857, it helped make pain relief in childbirth respectable, though doctors may already have been coming round.

myth.tradition: The operation was a flawless triumph, and Warren turned to the audience and declared, "Gentlemen, this is no humbug."
myth.record: Abbott's hospital notes do not even mention ether, and the anesthesia was incomplete. The famous line first appears in Morton's promotional biography of 1859, published after Warren's death, and no earlier evidence supports it.

links.note: Forty years earlier, a Japanese surgeon operated under a herbal general anesthetic.
John Snow, the leading anesthetist in London, also tracked cholera to a water pump.
Painless surgery allowed longer operations, making wound infection the next great problem.

title: Semmelweis and the washing of hands

confidence.note: The Vienna clinic's yearly mortality figures were published by Semmelweis himself and are not in doubt; the chlorine washing began around mid-May 1847. Why his colleagues resisted, and how he died, are argued over, and the popular picture of a lone genius ignored by fools is a simplification.

people: Ignaz Philipp Semmelweis (1818–1865), Hungarian obstetrician
Jakob Kolletschka, pathologist whose death gave Semmelweis the clue
Ferdinand von Hebra, dermatologist who first published the findings
Oliver Wendell Holmes (1809–1894), Boston physician who warned of contagion in 1843
summary: In a Vienna maternity clinic, women attended by doctors died at four times the rate of those attended by midwives. A basin of chlorine water closed the gap.
body: The Vienna General Hospital had two maternity clinics. Doctors and medical students worked in the first; midwives were trained in the second. When Ignaz Semmelweis was put in charge of the first clinic in July 1846, he found a grim difference: that year 459 of 4,010 women there died, mostly of childbed (puerperal) fever, against 105 of 3,754 in the midwives' clinic. Semmelweis tested and ruled out explanations one by one, from birthing positions to a priest's bell that frightened patients.

The clue came in 1847, when his colleague Jakob Kolletschka died of a fever like the mothers' after being cut by a student's scalpel during an autopsy. Doctors and students went straight from dissecting corpses to examining women in labor; midwives did not. Semmelweis concluded that "cadaverous particles" on the doctors' hands were killing them. Around mid-May 1847 he ordered everyone to wash in chlorinated lime before touching a patient. In 1848, the first full year of washing, deaths in the first clinic fell to 45 of 3,556, about 1.3 percent, the same as the midwives'.

He was not alone in seeing the danger. Alexander Gordon in Aberdeen had argued in the 1790s that the fever was carried from patient to patient, and in 1843 Oliver Wendell Holmes told Boston doctors much the same. What Semmelweis added was numbers. But he let others publish for him, first his friend Ferdinand von Hebra in December 1847, and his own book appeared only in 1861. Germ theory did not yet exist to explain why washing worked; many obstetricians blamed miasma or other causes, and the idea that physicians were killing their patients was unwelcome.

His own temper did not help: in print he called his opponents murderers. In 1865 he was taken to a newly built asylum in Vienna and died two weeks later of sepsis. Only after his death did Vienna start calling him the "savior of mothers."

myth.tradition: Semmelweis, a lone genius, was ignored purely out of prejudice, then died of childbed fever from a scalpel cut, killed by the very disease he had fought.
myth.record: Others had made similar arguments before him, he delayed publishing for years, and his insults alienated potential allies. Accounts of his death differ, but recent scholars attribute the fatal sepsis to wounds from rough treatment in the asylum rather than to a dissection cut.

links.note: Germ theory later explained why chlorine washing worked.
Lister brought antisepsis into surgery and admired Semmelweis.
Vienna's routine autopsies, the legacy of pathological anatomy, carried the infection.

title: John Snow and the Broad Street pump

confidence.note: Snow's own 1855 book and the parish inquiry document the Soho outbreak, the pump and the water-company comparison. What is disputed is the drama: the outbreak was already subsiding when the handle came off, and Snow's waterborne theory was not generally accepted until after his death.

people: John Snow (1813–1858), physician and anesthetist
Henry Whitehead, local clergyman who investigated the outbreak
Filippo Pacini, Florentine anatomist who described the cholera vibrio
summary: Over 500 people near one Soho street died of cholera in ten days. A doctor who thought the disease was swallowed, not breathed, pointed at the neighborhood pump.
body: In the night of 31 August 1854, cholera exploded around Broad Street, Golden Square, in Soho. In Snow's words, "there were upwards of five hundred fatal attacks of cholera in ten days" within 250 yards of one corner. Most doctors then blamed miasma, foul air rising from filth. John Snow, a London physician better known as an expert anesthetist, had argued since the epidemic of 1848–49 that cholera was caused by something swallowed, and spread by sewage-tainted water.

He mapped the deaths and found they clustered around the public pump in Broad Street. The exceptions fit too. A nearby workhouse with its own well lost only five of 535 inmates, and none of the 70-odd men at the Broad Street brewery fell ill; they drank beer and the brewery's own well water. Snow put his case to the parish Board of Guardians, and the pump handle was removed the next day. A local clergyman, Henry Whitehead, proved a sharp detective too, and identified a five-month-old girl as the probable first case.

Snow's stronger evidence came from south London, where two water companies supplied neighboring houses. Over seven weeks in 1854, houses served by the Southwark and Vauxhall Company, which drew water from a sewage-laden stretch of the Thames, suffered 315 cholera deaths per 10,000 houses; houses supplied by the Lambeth Company, which had moved its intake upstream, suffered 37. Snow published both studies in the second edition of *On the Mode of Communication of Cholera* in 1855.

The same year, in Florence, Filippo Pacini saw vast numbers of bacteria in the intestines of cholera victims and named them *Vibrio cholerae*. Neither man was widely believed. Pacini's work was largely ignored until Robert Koch found the organism again in 1884, and Snow's two investigations were cited as conclusive only after he died in 1858.

myth.tradition: Snow removed the pump handle himself and thereby stopped the epidemic in its tracks, converting the authorities to his theory.
myth.record: The parish authorities removed the handle at Snow's urging, by which time the outbreak was already subsiding. His waterborne theory was not generally accepted in his lifetime; his investigations were cited as conclusive only after his death.

links.note: Sanitary reformers who blamed foul air were Snow's main opponents.
Snow's other career was as London's leading anesthetist.
Koch's cholera bacillus of 1884 vindicated the waterborne theory.

title: Florence Nightingale's statistics

confidence.note: Her reports and diagrams were printed in 1858 and survive, as do the army's mortality figures. How much of the fall in deaths at Scutari was due to sanitation rather than other changes was questioned at the time, and her reputation has been shaped by legend in both directions.

people: Florence Nightingale (1820–1910), nurse, statistician and reformer
William Farr, statistician at the General Register Office who advised her
John Sutherland and Robert Rawlinson, members of the Sanitary Commission
Mary Seacole, Jamaican-born nurse and businesswoman in the Crimea
summary: The 'Lady with the Lamp' did her most lasting work after the war, with tables and colored wedges that showed the British Army it had been killing its own men with dirt.
body: Florence Nightingale reached Constantinople with her party of nurses on 3 November 1854 to run the nursing in the army hospital at Scutari. It was dirty, overcrowded and short of everything, and most of its patients were suffering from disease rather than wounds. Her nurses cleaned, cooked and washed linen. Yet by February 1855 the hospital's death rate had risen to 42 percent. Nightingale blamed poor nutrition; in fact the building sat on a broken sewer. In March 1855 a government Sanitary Commission led by Dr John Sutherland, with the engineer Robert Rawlinson, arrived, repaired drains and improved ventilation, and within weeks the death rate had fallen by half.

Back in England in August 1856, Nightingale drew her own lesson from the figures. With William Farr of the General Register Office she analyzed army mortality for a Royal Commission and in 1858 published the results, including in *Notes on Matters Affecting the Health, Efficiency and Hospital Administration of the British Army*. She showed that most of the army's deaths in the war came from sickness, that sanitation had reduced them, and that even soldiers stationed at home died at higher rates than ordinary civilian men. She also exposed the army's slack record-keeping, estimating that Crimean hospital returns might have shown only a seventh of the real deaths.

Her famous wedge diagrams were persuasion, not invention: William Playfair had published a pie chart in 1801. What was new was using graphics to argue for reform. She became the first female fellow of the Royal Statistical Society.

The public knew her as 'the Lady with the Lamp,' and in 1860 donations to the Nightingale Fund paid for a training school for nurses at St Thomas's Hospital in London. Another nurse of the war, the Jamaican-born Mary Seacole, was turned down by the War Office and by Nightingale's service, paid her own way to the Crimea and treated soldiers near the front line.

myth.tradition: Nightingale's nursing at Scutari slashed the death rate, and she invented the pie chart to prove it.
myth.record: Deaths at Scutari rose after her arrival and fell only after the Sanitary Commission repaired the sewers and ventilation, a cause she herself had at first misjudged. Statistical graphics, including pie charts, existed before her; her originality lay in using them to drive reform.

links.note: Counting the dead to find causes went back to Graunt's bills of mortality.
She shared the sanitarians' belief that filth and bad air caused disease.
In the same years Snow used death counts to trace cholera to water.
The Crimean War's suffering helped inspire organized care for wounded soldiers.

title: Virchow's cellular pathology

confidence.note: *Die Cellularpathologie*, based on lectures Virchow gave at the Charité in Berlin, was published in 1858. His famous principle borrowed from others, notably Robert Remak, whose credit is still argued over; and the 'social science' slogan is usually quoted from his 1848 reform writings rather than from this book.

people: Rudolf Virchow (1821–1902), pathologist and politician
Robert Remak, embryologist whose work on cell division Virchow built on
Theodor Schwann (1810–1882) and Matthias Schleiden (1804–1881), founders of cell theory
summary: A Berlin pathologist told doctors to 'think microscopically': disease lives in cells. Ten years earlier he had blamed a typhus epidemic on poverty and politics.
body: In 1858 Rudolf Virchow, the leading pathologist at Berlin's Charité hospital, published lectures he had given to doctors as *Die Cellularpathologie*. Schleiden and Schwann had argued in 1838–39 that plants and animals are built of cells. Virchow carried the idea into medicine: disease, he said, is a disturbance of cells, and can be diagnosed by looking at them under a microscope. His slogan *omnis cellula e cellula*, every cell comes from a cell, drew on the work of Robert Remak, whom he was slow to credit. The approach remains the basis of tissue diagnosis today.

Virchow was also a radical. Sent by the Prussian government to investigate typhus in Upper Silesia in 1847–48, he wrote a 190-page report blaming poverty and ignorance, and prescribed "full and unlimited democracy" and education rather than drugs. He joined the Berlin revolution of 1848, co-founded the weekly *Medical Reform*, and lost his post in 1849. Later a member of parliament and an opponent of Bismarck, he is quoted as saying that "medicine is a social science, and politics is nothing else but medicine on a large scale."

Morgagni located disease in organs; Virchow took it down to cells.

title: Pasteur and the germ theory

confidence.note: Pasteur's papers to the French Academy of Sciences fix the dates of his fermentation work (from 1857), the swan-necked flask experiments (published 1861) and his wine patent (1865). How much of the credit is his is contested: many predecessors and rivals made overlapping claims, and historians reading his notebooks have found him quick to claim priority.

people: Louis Pasteur (1822–1895), chemist and microbiologist
Antoine-Jérôme Balard (1802–1876), chemist and mentor who devised the swan-necked flask experiment
Félix-Archimède Pouchet (1800–1872), naturalist who defended spontaneous generation
Antoine Béchamp (1816–1908), chemist and rival
summary: A chemist asked to fix spoiled beet alcohol ended up showing that invisible living things ferment, spoil and rot, and that they come from other microbes, not from nowhere.
body: Louis Pasteur came to microbes through industry. As dean of the science faculty at Lille in the mid-1850s he was approached by makers of beet alcohol whose fermentations kept going wrong. Beginning in 1857 with a report on lactic fermentation, he argued before the French Academy of Sciences that fermentation is the work of living microorganisms, not a purely chemical breakdown. He was not the first to suspect this: Schwann, Cagniard de Latour and others had tied yeast to fermentation in the 1830s, and Antoine Béchamp reached similar conclusions shortly before him. But Pasteur pressed the case relentlessly.

If microbes caused fermentation, where did they come from? Many respected naturalists held that they could arise spontaneously, and in 1858 Félix Pouchet published experiments claiming to prove it. Pasteur's answer, compiled in a prize-winning memoir of 1861, used flasks with long, curving necks, an idea of his mentor Antoine-Jérôme Balard. Broth boiled in them and kept from the outside air stayed lifeless for months; once dust from the air reached it, microbes appeared within two or three days. The air, he concluded, carries germs. Pouchet was not instantly silenced, and the argument rumbled on for years.

The practical results came fast. In 1865 Pasteur patented a way to keep wine from spoiling by heating it to 64 °C for 30 minutes, later called pasteurization (the idea of heating wine went back to Nicolas Appert, and it was first applied to milk by Franz von Soxhlet). He then spent years on the diseases of silkworms, at first wrongly denying that a parasite was to blame.

His work persuaded the surgeon Joseph Lister that microbes from the air infected wounds. But proving that a particular microbe causes a particular human or animal disease came later, and from Germany: Robert Koch's work on anthrax in 1876.

myth.tradition: Pasteur alone discovered that germs cause fermentation and disease, and a single elegant flask experiment instantly killed the idea of spontaneous generation.
myth.record: Others had linked microbes to fermentation before him, the flask design came from Balard, and the dispute over spontaneous generation continued into the 1870s. The first proof that a microbe causes a specific disease is usually credited to Koch in 1876.

Germ theory explained why Semmelweis's chlorine washing had worked.
Lister read Pasteur and turned germ theory into antiseptic surgery.
Koch proved that specific microbes cause specific diseases.

title: The Red Cross and the Geneva Convention

confidence.note: The founding meetings of 1863 and the signing of the Geneva Convention on 22 August 1864 are fully documented. Casualty figures for Solferino vary between accounts.

people: Henry Dunant (1828–1910), Swiss businessman and founder of the Red Cross
summary: A Swiss businessman stumbled onto a battlefield strewn with untended wounded, wrote a book about it, and within five years a dozen states had signed a treaty to protect medics.
body: On 24 June 1859 Henry Dunant, a Swiss businessman, reached Solferino in northern Italy after one of the century's bloodiest battles and helped tend the wounded in nearby Castiglione. His book *A Memory of Solferino* (1862) proposed volunteer relief societies in every nation. In February 1863 a Geneva committee of five, the future International Committee of the Red Cross, adopted it, and on 22 August 1864 twelve nations signed the first Geneva Convention, protecting medical staff under a red cross on white. Dunant went bankrupt in 1867 but shared the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.

links.note: The Crimean War had already exposed the neglect of wounded soldiers.

title: Mendel's peas

confidence.note: Mendel's lectures (1865) and paper (1866) survive in print. That his numbers fit his predicted ratios suspiciously well was argued by R. A. Fisher in 1936 and is still debated; the laws themselves are not in doubt.

people: Gregor Mendel (1822–1884), Augustinian friar and later abbot
Carl Nägeli, Swiss botanist who corresponded with him
Ronald A. Fisher, statistician who questioned his data in 1936
summary: A friar crossing garden peas found that traits pass down as separate units in predictable ratios. Almost nobody noticed for 34 years.
body: In February and March 1865 the friar Gregor Mendel read two lectures on his crosses of garden peas to the Natural History Society of Brünn (now Brno), which printed them in 1866. Following seven traits, each in two forms, he showed that they were inherited as separate units in predictable ratios. The botanist Carl Nägeli was unimpressed, Mendel became abbot in 1868, and the paper was little read until 1900, when Hugo De Vries and others rediscovered it. In 1936 the statistician R. A. Fisher argued that the results fit too well to be honest; pea geneticists still disagree.

links.note: The units Mendel inferred turned out to be stretches of DNA.
